entry.title: Unit 5 - Vocabulary, Grammar & Reflection

author.name: Keny Calderin, Valentina Cabrales, Angelica Bravo, Dayana Atencia

entry.summary: This unit focuses on sports and the use of past modal verbs (could have, should have, would have) to discuss hypothetical situations. Click here to review all the content and my interactive reflection.
entry.content:
Vocabulary

Word Definition Example Sentence Image
regret a feeling of sadness or disappointment about something that happened, or that you wish had been different She still feels regret about missing the final match due to an injury.
nevertheless in spite of what was just said; however The task seemed impossible; nevertheless, the team managed to finish it on time.
assumption something you believe to be true without checking it Making the wrong assumption about what my teammate meant caused a big misunderstanding.
possibility a chance that something might happen or be true There's still a possibility that the team could have won if they hadn't made that mistake.
revival the return of interest in something that had become less popular The revival of board games happened partly because people wanted more face-to-face contact.
misunderstanding a failure to understand something correctly, causing confusion Their misunderstanding about the deadline caused the whole project to be delayed.
clarify to make something clearer or easier to understand Could you clarify what you meant by "send it soon"?
excerpt a short section taken from a longer text, speech, or recording We listened to an excerpt from the radio show to practice understanding new words.
vary to be different or to change from one situation to another Athletes' earnings can vary a great deal depending on the sport and the country.
restate to say something again, usually in clearer or different words In her conclusion, she restated her opinion using different words.
stood a chance had a real possibility of succeeding or winning Nobody thought the underdog team stood a chance against the world champions.
tournament a series of contests between many players or teams Thousands of fans watched the e-sports tournament live in the stadium.
sponsorship financial support given to an event, team, or person, usually for advertising The team could travel to the championship thanks to a sponsorship from a tech company.
gifted having a natural, often exceptional, ability or talent Even highly gifted people in other professions often earn far less than top athletes.
delighted feeling great pleasure or happiness I was delighted to finally understand the joke once someone explained the new word.
hidden kept out of sight or not easily noticed The players had to find the hidden treasures before the island sank.
profits the financial gain made from a business activity Top athletes' salaries are often justified by the profits they generate through advertising.
contract a written legal agreement between two or more parties The player signed a sponsorship contract worth millions of dollars.
broadcast to send out a program on TV, radio, or online The championship game was broadcast live in over fifty countries.
contradict to say or show that something is not true, or to disagree with someone The new evidence seemed to contradict everything the coach had said earlier.

Grammar: Could have, should have, and would have

What it is / what it's for:

These are past modal verbs used to talk about hypothetical past situations — things that were possible but didn't happen, things you now wish had been different, or imagined results of a different past action.

When it is used:

  • Could have + past participle → to talk about past possibility or ability that wasn't used.

  • Should have / shouldn't have + past participle → to talk about regrets, things that were the right or wrong thing to do, but didn't happen that way.

  • Would have + past participle → to talk about an imagined result in the past, usually connected to an unreal past condition.

Structure / Rule

Subject + modal (could / should / would) + have + past participle

  • Affirmative form: Subject + modal + have + past participle

    • She could have won the match, but she got injured.

  • Negative form: Subject + modal + not (couldn't / shouldn't / wouldn't) + have + past participle

    • He shouldn't have missed that easy shot.

  • Interrogative form: Modal + subject + have + past participle?

    • Could she have scored if she had jumped higher?

Three original sentences:

  1. I could have finished the project earlier if I had started studying sooner.

  2. You shouldn't have told her the surprise before the party.

  3. If the team had trained harder, they would have won the championship.

Reflection

Click here to read the unit reflection.
In this unit, I learned a lot of new vocabulary related to sports, competition, and games, as well as how to use past modal verbs like could have, should have, and would have to talk about regrets and past possibilities. I also developed my listening skills by using context to understand new words, and I practiced communicating clearly in a group to avoid misunderstandings.

One activity I found difficult was writing the opinion essay, because I had trouble structuring my paragraphs clearly and connecting opposing points of view using linking words. I also need to improve my pronunciation of stressed syllables, especially in words like compete and competitive. To improve these difficulties, I plan to practice writing short paragraphs every day and record myself speaking to check my pronunciation and fluency.

entry.title: Unit 3 - Vocabulary, Grammar & Reflection

author.name: Keny Calderin, Valentina Cabrales, Angelica Bravo, Dayana Atencia

entry.summary: In this unit, we focus on future predictions, well-being, and personal goals. Click here to view the vocabulary, the rules for using "will," and my interactive reflection.
entry.content:
Vocabulary

Word Definition Example Image
Prosperous Successful and doing well. I want to have a prosperous career.
Litter Trash left in a public place. People should not leave litter on the beach.
Upcycle To reuse something to make it useful again. I like to upcycle old clothes.
Therapeutic Something that helps you feel better or relaxed. Music can be therapeutic when I feel stressed.
Predict To say what you think will happen in the future. It is difficult to predict the future.
Gradually Slowly, little by little. My English is gradually improving.
Sharp growth A quick and big increase. There has been sharp growth in technology.
Continue To keep doing something. I want to continue studying English.
Estimate To make an approximate calculation. I estimate that I will finish tomorrow.
Remain unchanged To stay the same. Some traditions may remain unchanged.
Feedback Comments that help someone improve. My teacher gave me useful feedback.
Improve To become better. I want to improve my English.
Opinion An idea or belief about something. Everyone has a different opinion.
Achieve To successfully reach a goal. I want to achieve my goals.
Strength A good quality or ability. One of my strengths is being responsible.
Weakness Something you need to improve. Speaking is one of my weaknesses.
Motivate To make someone want to do something. My family motivates me to study.
Well-being Being healthy and feeling good. Exercise is good for my well-being.
Goal Something you want to achieve. My goal is to speak English better.
Constructive Helpful for improving something. My teacher gave me constructive feedback.

Grammar: Making Predictions

We use different forms to talk about the future and make predictions.

WILL

We use "will" for future predictions.

  • Structure: Subject + will + verb
  • Example: People will use more technology in the future.
  • Negative: Subject + will not + verb
  • Example: People will not stop using technology.

Reflection

Click here to read the unit reflection.
Unit 3 was about the future, predictions, feedback, and personal goals. I learned new vocabulary and how to use will, be going to, may, and might to talk about the future. I also learned that feedback can help me improve. This unit was useful because I can use these topics to talk about my plans and goals. I will continue practicing my English, especially speaking and pronunciation.

entry.title: Unit 2 - Vocabulary

author.name: Keny Calderin, Valentina Cabrales, Angelica Bravo, Dayana Atencia

entry.summary: In this unit, we explore essential vocabulary for daily communication, as well as common rules and actions. Click here to view the complete table with images and examples.
entry.content:
Vocabulary List

# Word Definition Example Sentence Image
1 Twice Two times I brush my teeth twice a day.
2 Pigeon A gray bird that lives in cities There are many pigeons in the park.
3 Banned Not allowed by a rule or law Smoking is banned in the restaurant.
4 Instead In the place of something else I didn't drink coffee, I drank tea instead.
5 Lawmakers People who make the laws of a country The lawmakers voted for a new law.
6 Glance To look at something quickly She glanced at her watch before leaving.
7 Kite A toy that flies in the wind on a long string The children are flying a kite on the beach.
8 Windy When there is a lot of wind It is very windy today, so wear a jacket.
9 Creep To move slowly and quietly The cat creeps toward the bird.
10 Apologize To say "I'm sorry" I want to apologize for being late.
11 Terraces Flat open areas outside a building or on a hill The hotel has beautiful terraces with a view of the sea.
12 Outlawed Made illegal by law That dangerous drug was outlawed many years ago.
13 Whistling Making a sound by blowing air through your lips My dad is whistling a song in the kitchen.
14 Forbidden Not permitted It is forbidden to swim in this lake.
15 Seem To look like or appear to be You seem tired today.
16 Backed Supported by someone Her idea was backed by the whole team.
17 Whisper To speak very quietly She whispered a secret in my ear.
18 Yell To speak very loudly Don't yell, the baby is sleeping.
19 Rush To do something or go somewhere very quickly I had to rush to catch the bus.
20 Switch To change from one thing to another Can you switch seats with me?

Grammar — making predictions

Talking about the past in English isn't always straightforward; sometimes we discuss events that happened one after another, while at other times, one action was already underway when another interrupted it. We might also need to speak about something that occurred prior to another past event or even imagine a different past that never actually happened.

To express all of this correctly, English uses three main past tenses: the simple past, the past continuous, and the past perfect. Each serves a specific function, and knowing which one to use helps us tell a story clearly and convey the correct sequence of events.

Simple Past

We use the simple past when one thing happens, and then another thing happens right after it. The actions are in order, like a list.

• I backed up my computer, then I shut it down

More examples:

• I woke up, had breakfast, and left the house.

• She opened the door and turned on the lights.

Past Continuous

We use the past continuous for a longer action that was happening in the past. Then, a shorter action (in simple past) interrupts it. • I realized someone was using my bank account when I saw $200 mysteriously disappear

Structure: was/were + verb-ing (long action) + simple past (short action that interrupts)

More examples:

• I was watching TV when the phone rang.

• They were walking home when it started to rain.

Past Perfect

We use the past perfect to show that something happened before another past event. It shows the first action in a sequence of two past actions.

• I didn't buy those things. Someone had copied my card. Structure: had + past participle

More examples:

• When I arrived at the station, the train had already left.

• She was tired because she had worked all night.

Past Perfect

We also use the past perfect when we report (retell) what someone said. If the person originally used the simple past or the present perfect, we change it to past perfect in reported speech.

• He asked me whether I had ever been the victim of an online crime.

(Original question: "Have you ever been the victim of an online crime?")

More examples:

• She said she had finished the project. (Original: "I have finished the project.")

• He told me he had seen that movie. (Original: "I saw that movie.")

Past Perfect

We use the past perfect to imagine a different past — something that didn't really happen. This is often used with "if" to talk about regrets or imaginary results.

• If the bank hadn't blocked my card so quickly, I would have lost it all!

Structure: If + past perfect, ... would have + past participle

More examples:

• If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.

• If she hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have been late.

Reflection

Click here to read the unit reflection.
Throughout this course, I have gained important knowledge and skills, particularly in grammar, vocabulary, and listening comprehension. I learned to use various past tenses more accurately and expanded my vocabulary through reading and class discussions. Activities such as group work, listening exercises, and writing short stories helped me practice speaking and improve my writing skills. However, I faced some challenges especially in understanding rapid speech and natural pronunciation, as well as in confidently using more complex grammatical structures in real conversations. I also realized that I need to continue expanding my vocabulary and become more comfortable speaking spontaneously.

To address these challenges, I plan to regularly listen to English podcasts and watch videos, review grammar topics on my own, and seek out more opportunities to speak English, even outside of class. I believe that with consistent practice, I will continue to make steady progress.
